key: Then the soul will be a negative existence, passively responsive to externals. In such a negative existence, only TAO can abide. And that negative state is the fasting of the heart.”
s: Counselling Yen Hui before he goes to the headstrong Prince of Wei, Confucius explains a fast; Guo Xiang, on chapter 4, reads it as setting aside ears, eyes, mind and intent, trusting the breath’s own nature, for in an emptied heart the utmost Way gathers.
src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 4, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 5, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907034 (2026)

evidence.words: 遺耳目，去心意，而付氣性之自得，此虛以待物者也…虛其心則至道集於懷也。
evidence.gloss: [On the breath, empty and waiting on things:] Leave ears and eyes, drop mind and intent, and entrust all to the breath-nature attaining of itself: this is being empty and waiting on things. … [On the Way gathering in emptiness:] Empty the heart, and the utmost Way gathers in one’s bosom.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Zhuangzi 4.38, at 291), beginning at a sentence start inside the unit. Plain sense faithful: Confucius counsels Yen Hui, bound for the Prince of Wei whom 4.7 calls of an unmanageable disposition. Guo Xiang’s notes on exactly the key verse’s Chinese lines (氣也者，虛而待物者也; 唯道集虛) say to leave ears and eyes, drop mind and intent, entrust all to the breath’s own attaining, and that in an emptied heart the utmost Way gathers; the reading follows these without drift. The packet prints a stray 他 after 者也; the evidence stops before it. Revision 7907034 dated 2026-07-06 by the Wikisource API. entry-check ok.
